The Story of Suvrat Muni

I bow to Lord Jina, whose feet are worshipped by the gods, and I write the story of Suvrat Muni.

In the beautiful city of Dwaraka in the Saurashtra region, the last Narayan, Shrikrishna, was born. Shrikrishna had many wives, but among them all, Satyabhama was the most fortunate. Shrikrishna's greatest love was for her. Shrikrishna was the half-chakravartin, lord of three continents. Thousands of kings and maharajas were always present in his service.

One day, Shrikrishna was going to the Samavasaran to see Lord Neminath. On the way, he saw the ascetic Shri Suvrat Muni in a diseased state. His entire body was suffering from illness. Shrikrishna could not bear to see his condition. His heart was stirred with religious love. He immediately called a famous physician named Jivak and, showing him the monk, asked for medicine. According to the physician's instructions, he had laddoos mixed with medicine made in all the shravakas' homes. Within a few days, through this arrangement, the monk recovered, and his entire body became as beautiful as before. Through the power of this gift of medicine, Shrikrishna bound the karma that determines the nature of a Tirthankara. Truly, through giving to worthy recipients for the sake of happiness, the noble attain everything in this world.

Seeing Suvrat Muni in a healthy state one day, Shrikrishna was very pleased, for he had succeeded in his purpose. He asked him, "Lord, are you well now?" The monk replied, "O King, the body is by nature impure, perishable, and changing every moment through various states. What is good or bad in it? Just as change is the nature of things, so this body is sometimes healthy and sometimes diseased. Yes, I feel neither sorrow in being diseased nor joy in being healthy. I am engaged only with the soul, which I am striving to attain and which is my supreme duty."

Seeing Suvrat yogiraj's such detachment from the body, Shrikrishna was greatly delighted. He bowed to the monk and praised him highly.

But when this detachment of the monk reached the ears of Jivak the physician, he was greatly distressed — rather, he felt extreme contempt for the monk, thinking, "I did so much good for this monk, yet he shows no gratitude." This shows the difference between worldly and spiritual perspectives. The physician expected gratitude, but the monk, being detached from the body, saw no reason for either sorrow or joy in its condition.

This story teaches the supreme value of compassion and service. Shrikrishna's act of arranging medicine for the sick monk earned him the karma of a Tirthankara. And the monk's detachment from bodily conditions shows the highest spiritual state — equanimity in health and illness alike. The wise should serve the sick with compassion, while those on the spiritual path should remain equanimous in the face of bodily changes.
